reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: An acquired condition of the natal cleft in which loose hairs are driven into the skin, provoking a foreign-body reaction and forming midline pits and a chronic sinus
Typically affects young, hirsute men, and is associated with a deep natal cleft, sedentary occupations, obesity, and poor local hygiene
May present acutely as a painful fluctuant abscess or chronically with intermittent discharge and one or more midline pits, often with lateral secondary openings
Characteristic midline pits in the intergluteal cleft, sometimes containing protruding hair tufts, are the diagnostic hallmark
Acute abscesses are treated by incision and drainage placed off the midline; definitive treatment of the sinus follows once inflammation settles

Definitive options range from minimally invasive (pit picking, phenol or laser ablation) to excision with off-midline or flap closure (Karydakis, Bascom cleft-lift, Limberg flap), which flatten the cleft and reduce recurrence
Hair removal, hygiene, and keeping the cleft clean and dry reduce recurrence after treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Pilonidal disease is now regarded as acquired rather than congenital. Friction and movement in the natal cleft, together with a hair-friendly microenvironment, allow shed hairs to penetrate the skin through enlarged follicles or midline pits. The embedded hair acts as a foreign body, provoking chronic inflammation, granulation, and a sinus lined by granulation tissue that discharges and can abscess. A deep cleft, hirsutism, obesity, and prolonged sitting perpetuate the cycle, and midline wounds that heal poorly predispose to recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Perianal or anal fistula tracking towards the natal cleft
Furuncle, carbuncle, or infected sebaceous cyst
Presacral sinus or osteomyelitis with cutaneous discharge
additionalInvestigations: Clinical inspection of the natal cleft for midline pits and secondary tracks
Examination under anaesthesia with probing for complex or recurrent disease
MRI in atypical, recurrent, or extensive disease to map tracks
Assessment for Crohn's disease when perianal features are atypical
Swab and culture of discharge if secondary infection is suspected
Biopsy of chronic, non-healing lesions to exclude malignant change
redFlags: A chronic non-healing sinus with induration or a mass suggesting malignant (squamous) change
Extensive or atypical tracks suggesting Crohn's disease or hidradenitis suppurativa
Rapidly spreading sepsis in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient
A fistulous communication with the anal canal
reference.prognosis: Pilonidal disease is prone to recurrence, particularly with midline wounds and persistent risk factors; off-midline closure techniques and diligent hair control substantially improve long-term healing.
pitfalls: Closing wounds in the midline, which heal poorly and recur
Neglecting hair removal and hygiene advice after surgery
Mistaking a pilonidal track for an anal fistula, or the reverse
Overlooking rare malignant transformation in long-standing disease
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Keighley & Williams' Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon
